name: Simonides of Ceos
bio: Simonides of Ceos (c. 556 – 468 BC) was one of the great lyric poets of Greece and the most famous composer of epitaphs and dedicatory epigrams, among them the lines on the Greek dead of the Persian Wars. Many of the epigrams that circulated under his name are not his.
The epigrams here are those that Paton's first volume ascribes to him, a few of them with doubt.

poems.title: Book V, 159
poems.author: Simonides of Ceos
poems.text: Borpron, the flute-player, and Pythias, both most lovable once upon a time, dedicate to thee, Cypris, these zones and pictures. Merchant and skipper, thy purse knows whence the zones and whence the pictures.

poems.title: Book VI, 2
poems.author: Simonides of Ceos
poems.text: This bow, resting from tearful war, hangs here under the roof of Athene’s temple. Often mid the roar of battle, in the struggle of men, was it washed in the blood of Persian cavaliers.

poems.title: Book VI, 50: On the Altar at Plataea commemorating the Battle
poems.author: Simonides of Ceos
poems.text: This altar of Zeus the Liberator did the Hellenes erect, an ornament for Hellas such as becomes a free land, after that, obeying their brave hearts’ impulse, they had driven out the Persians by the might of their hands and by the toil of battle.

poems.title: Book VI, 52
poems.author: Simonides of Ceos
poems.text: Rest, my long lance, thus against the high column and remain sacred to Panomphaean Zeus. For now thy point is old, and thou art worn by long brandishing in the battle.

poems.title: Book VI, 197
poems.author: Simonides of Ceos
poems.text: I, Pausantas, the leader of the Greeks, dedicated this monument to Phoebus, when I destroyed the army of the Medes.”

poems.title: Book VI, 212
poems.author: Simonides of Ceos
poems.text: Pray, Cyton, that the god, the son of Leto, who presides over the market-place, scene of beautiful dances, may take joy in thy gifts as great as is the praise thou receivest by the gifts to thee of crowns loaded with gratitude from strangers and citizens of Corinth.

poems.title: Book VI, 213
poems.author: Simonides of Ceos
poems.text: Six and fifty bulls and as many tripods didst thou win, Simonides, ere thou didst dedicate this tablet. Even so many times, after teaching thy odes to the delightsome chorus of men, didst thou mount the splendid chariot of glorious victory.

poems.title: Book VI, 214
poems.author: Simonides of Ceos
poems.text: I say that Gelo, Hiero, Polyzelus, and Thrasybulus, the sons of Dinomenes, dedicated the tr ipod I weighing talents and six hundred litrae of Damaretian gold, a tithe of the tithe.

poems.title: Book VI, 215
poems.author: Simonides of Ceos
poems.text: These shields, won from their foes the Medes, the sailors of Diodorus dedicated to Leto in memory of the sea-fight.®

poems.title: Book VI, 216
poems.author: Simonides of Ceos
poems.text: Sosus and Soso dedicated this (tripod) in thanks for being so saved, Sosus because he was so saved and Soso because Sosus was so saved.

poems.title: Book VI, 217
poems.author: Simonides of Ceos
poems.text: The priest of Rhea, when taking shelter from the winter snow-storm he entered the lonely cave, had just wiped the snow off his hair, when following on his steps came a lion, devourer of cattle, into the hollow way. But he with outspread hand beat the great tambour he held and the whole cave rang with the sound. Nor did that woodland beast dare to support the holy boom of Cybele, but rushed straight up the forest-clad hill, in dread of the half-girlish servant of the goddess, who hath dedicated to her these robes and this his yellow hair.

poems.title: Book VII, 24: On the Same
poems.author: Simonides of Ceos
poems.text: O vine who soothest all, nurse of wine, mother of the grape, thou who dost put forth thy web of curling tendrils, flourish green in the fine soil and climb up the pillar of the grave of Teian Anacreon; that he, the reveller heavy with wine, playing all through the night on his lad-loving lyre, may even as he lies low in earth have the glorious ripe clusters hanging from the branches over his head, and that he may be ever steeped in the dew that scented the old man’s tender lips so sweetly.

poems.title: Book VII, 25: On the Same
poems.author: Simonides of Ceos
poems.text: In this tomb of Teos, his home, was Anacreon laid, the singer whom the Muses made deathless, who set to the sweet love of lads measures breathing of the Graces, breathing of Love. Alone in Acheron he grieves not that he has left the sun and dwelleth there in the house of Lethe, but that he has left Megisteus, graceful above all the youth, and his passion for Thracian Smerdies. Yet never doth he desist from song delightful as honey, and even in Hades he hath not laid that lute to rest.

poems.title: Book VII, 77: On Simonides (?)
poems.author: Simonides of Ceos
poems.text: The saviour of the Ceian Simonides is this man, who even in death requited him who lived.

poems.title: Book VII, 177
poems.author: Simonides of Ceos
poems.text: This monument his father erected above Spinther on his death (the rest is missing).

poems.title: Book VII, 248
poems.author: Simonides of Ceos
poems.text: Four thousand from Peloponnesus once fought here with three millions.

poems.title: Book VII, 249
poems.author: Simonides of Ceos
poems.text: Stranger, bear this message to the Spartans, that we lie here obedient to their laws.

poems.title: Book VII, 250
poems.author: Simonides of Ceos
poems.text: We lie here, having given our lives to save all Hellas when she stood on a razor’s edge.

poems.title: Book VII, 251
poems.author: Simonides of Ceos
poems.text: These men having clothed their dear country in inextinguishable glory, donned the dark cloud of death; and having died, yet they are not dead, for their valour’s renown brings them up from the house of Hades.

poems.title: Book VII, 253
poems.author: Simonides of Ceos
poems.text: If to die well be the chief part of virtue, Fortune granted this to us above all others; for striving to endue Hellas with freedom, we lie here possessed of praise that groweth not old.

poems.title: Book VII, 254
poems.author: Simonides of Ceos
poems.text: Hail, ye champions who won great glory in war, ye sons of Athens, excellent horsemen; who once for your country of fair dancing-floors lost your young lives, fighting against a great part of the Greeks.

poems.title: Book VII, 254b
poems.author: Simonides of Ceos
poems.text: I, Brotachus, a Gortynian of Crete, lie here, where I came not for this end, but to trade.

poems.title: Book VII, 258
poems.author: Simonides of Ceos
poems.text: This—E men once by the Eurymedon lost their bright youth, fighting with the front ranks of the Median bowmen, both on foot and from the swift ships; and dying they left behind them the glorious record of their courage.

poems.title: Book VII, 270
poems.author: Simonides of Ceos
poems.text: These men, when bringing the firstfruits from Sparta to Phoebus, one sea, one night, one ship brought to the grave.

poems.title: Book VII, 296
poems.author: Simonides of Ceos
poems.text: Since the sea parted Europe from Asia, since fierce Ares directs the battles of nations, never was a more splendid deed of arms performed by mortals on land and on the sea at once. For these men after slaying many Medes in Cyprus, took a hundred Phoenician ships at sea with their crews. Asia groaned aloud, smitten with both hands by their triumphant might.”

poems.title: Book VII, 300
poems.author: Simonides of Ceos
poems.text: Here the earth covers Pythonax and his brother, before they saw the prime of their lovely youth. Their father, Megaristus, set up this monument to them dead, an immortal gift to his mortal sons.

poems.title: Book VII, 301
poems.author: Simonides of Ceos
poems.text: Leonidas, King of spacious Sparta, illustrious are they who died with thee and are buried here. They faced in battle with the Medes the force of multitudinous bows and of steeds fleet of foot.

poems.title: Book VII, 302
poems.author: Simonides of Ceos
poems.text: Every man grieves at the death of those near to him, but his friends and the city regret (?) Nicodicus.

poems.title: Book VII, 344
poems.author: Simonides of Ceos
poems.text: I am the most valiant of beasts, and most valiant of men is he whom I guard standing on this stone tomb.

poems.title: Book VII, 348
poems.author: Simonides of Ceos
poems.text: Here I lie, Timocreon of Rhodes, after drinking much and eating much and speaking much ill of men.

poems.title: Book VII, 442
poems.author: Simonides of Ceos
poems.text: Let us ever remember the men whose tomb this is, who turned not from the battle but fell in arms before their city, defending Tegea rich in flocks, that Greece should never strip from their dead heads the crown of freedom.

poems.title: Book VII, 443
poems.author: Simonides of Ceos
poems.text: Once in the breasts of these men did Ares wash with red rain his long-barbed arrows. Instead of men who stood and faced the shafts this earth covers memorials of the dead, lifeless memorials of their living selves.

poems.title: Book VII, 496
poems.author: Simonides of Ceos
poems.text: Lofty Gerania, evil cliff, would that from the far Scythian land thou didst look down on the Danube and the long course of the Tanais, and didst not dwell near the waves of the Scironian sea and by the ravines of snowy Methurias. Now he is in the sea, a cold corpse, and the empty tomb here laments his unhappy voyage.

poems.title: Book VII, 507a
poems.author: Simonides of Ceos
poems.text: Thou seest not the grave of Croesus, but a poor labourer’s tomb is this, yet sufficient for me.

poems.title: Book VII, 507b
poems.author: Simonides of Ceos
poems.text: I, Gorgippus, without having looked on the bridal bed, descended to the chamber that none may escape of fair-haired Persephone.

poems.title: Book VII, 508
poems.author: Simonides of Ceos
poems.text: His city Gela buried here Pausanias, son of Anchites, a physician of the race of Asclepius, bearing a name expressive of his calling, who turned aside from the chambers of Persephone many men wasted by chilling disease.

poems.title: Book VII, 509
poems.author: Simonides of Ceos
poems.text: I am the monument of Theognis of Sinope, erected over him by Glaucus for the sake of their long companionship.

poems.title: Book VII, 510
poems.author: Simonides of Ceos
poems.text: The earth of a strange land lies on thy body, Cleisthenes, but the doom of death overtook thee wandering on the Euxine sea. Thou wast cheated of sweet, honied home-coming, nor ever didst thou return to sea-girt Chios.

poems.title: Book VII, 511
poems.author: Simonides of Ceos
poems.text: When I look on the tomb of Megacles dead, I pity thee, poor Callias, for what thou hast suffered.

poems.title: Book VII, 512
poems.author: Simonides of Ceos
poems.text: Through the valour of these men the smoke of spacious Tegea in flames never went up to heaven. They resolved to leave to their children their city prospering in freedom and to die themselves in the forefront of the fight.

poems.title: Book VII, 513
poems.author: Simonides of Ceos
poems.text: Protomachus said, when his father was holding him in his arms as he breathed forth his lovely youth, “Timenorides, never shalt thou cease to regret thy dear son’s valour and virtue.”

poems.title: Book VII, 514
poems.author: Simonides of Ceos
poems.text: Shame of retreat led Cleodemus, too, to mournful death when on the banks of ever-flowing Theaerus he engaged the Thracian troop, and his warrior son made the name of his father, Diphilus, famous.

poems.title: Book VII, 515
poems.author: Simonides of Ceos
poems.text: Alas, cruel sickness, why dost thou grudge the souls of men their sojourn with lovely youth? Timarchus, too, in his youth thou hast robbed of his sweet life ere he looked on a wedded wife.

poems.title: Book VII, 516
poems.author: Simonides of Ceos
poems.text: Zeus, Protector of strangers, let them who slew me meet with the same fate, but may they who laid me in earth live and prosper.

poems.title: Book VII, 647
poems.author: Simonides of Ceos
poems.note: Attribution doubtful in Paton (Simonides or Simias).
poems.text: These were the very last words that Gorgo spoke to her dear mother, in tears throwing her hands round her neck: “Stay here with father and mayest thou bear another daughter, more fortunate than I was, to tend thy grey old age.”

poems.title: Book VII, 677
poems.author: Simonides of Ceos
poems.text: This is the tomb of famous Megistias the prophet, whom the Persians slew after crossing the Spercheius. Though he well knew then the impending fate, he disdained to desert the Spartan leaders.

poems.title: Book IX, 700
poems.author: Simonides of Ceos
poems.text: Polygnotus of Thasos, the son of Aglaophon, painted the sack of the citadel of Troy.

poems.title: Book IX, 757
poems.author: Simonides of Ceos
poems.text: Ipuron of Corinth painted this. There is no fault in his hand, since the achievement far excels the expectation.

poems.title: Book IX, 758
poems.author: Simonides of Ceos
poems.text: Cimon painted the door on the right, and Dionysius that on the right as you go out.

poems.title: Book X, 105
poems.author: Simonides of Ceos
poems.text: A certain Theodorus rejoices because I am dead. Another shall rejoice at his death. We are all owed to death.

poems.title: Book XIII, 11
poems.author: Simonides of Ceos
poems.text: A. Who dedicated this portrait? B. Dorieus of Thurii. A. Was he not a Rhodian by descent? B. Yea, before he was exiled from his country. Many deeds of might he had done by his terrible hand.

poems.title: Book XIII, 14
poems.author: Simonides of Ceos
poems.note: Paton’s metre label: ‘Hexameter followed by a pentameter, two iambic trimeters, and a hexameter’.
poems.text: Here lies Dandes of Argos, the stadion racer, who gained honour by his victories for his fatherland, rich in pasture for horses. Twice did he conquer at Olympia, thrice at Delphi, twice at the Isthmus, and fifteen times at Nemea, and it is not easy to count his other victories.

poems.title: Book XIII, 19
poems.author: Simonides of Ceos
poems.note: Paton’s metre label: ‘Hexameters followed by verses of nine syllables’.
poems.text: This statue is the offering of Nicoladas of Corinth, who conquered at Delphi in the foot-race, and at the Panathenaea gained prizes, jars of oil, in five contests one after another; and in holy Isthmus the shore of the Sea-lord witnessed him win the prize thrice in succession; and in Nemea he gained three victories, another four in Pellene, and two in the precinct of Zeus Lycaeus; and likewise in Tegea, and in mighty Epidaurus, and in Thebes, and the land of Megara; and in Phlius, winning the stadion and pentathlon, he made great Corinth rejoice.

poems.title: Book XIII, 20
poems.author: Simonides of Ceos
poems.note: Paton’s metre label: ‘Hexameters followed alternately by a comic tetrameter wanting two syllables and an Archilochian scazon trimeter’.
poems.text: Oris, giving glory to his fatherland, the holy city of Athena, offered this pleasant flute, child of the black earth, that he wrought by the help of Hephaestus, to Aphrodite, having been vanquished by love for beautiful Bryson.

poems.title: Book XIII, 26
poems.author: Simonides of Ceos
poems.note: Paton’s metre label: ‘The same tetrameter followed by an imperfect trimeter’.
poems.text: I will tell of her; for it is not meet that she should lie here without a name, the noble wife of Archenautes, Xanthippe, granddaughter of Periander, him who once ruled over the people, holding the lordship of high-towered Corinth.

poems.title: Book XIII, 30
poems.author: Simonides of Ceos
poems.note: Paton’s metre label: ‘Hexameter, becoming a trochaic tetrameter by shifting the words’.
poems.text: Sing me, Muse, the son of fair-ankled Alcmene.

poems.title: Book XVI, 2
poems.author: Simonides of Ceos
poems.text: Know Theognetus when thou lookest on him, the boy who conquered at Olympia, the dexterous charioteer of wrestling, most lovely to behold, but in combat nowise inferior to his beauty. He won a crown for the city of his noble fathers.

poems.title: Book XVI, 3
poems.author: Simonides of Ceos
poems.text: Diophon, the son of Philo, was victor at the Isthmian and Pythian games in jumping, fleetness of foot, throwing the quoit, throwing the javelin, and wrestling.

poems.title: Book XVI, 23
poems.author: Simonides of Ceos
poems.text: A. Say who thou art, whose son, from what country, and in what a victor. B. Casmylus, son of Evagoras, a Rhodian, victor in boxing at the Pythian games.

poems.title: Book XVI, 24
poems.author: Simonides of Ceos
poems.text: This is a beautiful statue of beautiful Milo, who, by the banks of Pisa, conquered seven times and never once fell on his knees.

poems.title: Book XVI, 26
poems.author: Simonides of Ceos
poems.text: We fell under the fold of Dirphys, and our funeral mound was raised near the Euripus by our country. And not undeservedly: for we lost our delightful youth facing the rugged cloud of battle.

poems.title: Book XVI, 60
poems.author: Simonides of Ceos
poems.text: A. Who is this? B. A Bacchant. A. And who carved her? B. Scopas. A. And who made her frenzied, Bacchus or Scopas? B. Scopas.

poems.title: Book XVI, 82
poems.author: Simonides of Ceos
poems.text: Chares of Lindus made the Colossus of Rhodes, eighty cubits high.

poems.title: Book XVI, 232: On the Statue of Pan erected by Miltiades
poems.author: Simonides of Ceos
poems.text: Miltiades erected me, goat-footed Pan, the Arcadian, the foe of the Medes, the friend of the Athenians.

poems.title: Of the Athenian Dead at Plataea (Mackail)
poems.author: Simonides of Ceos
poems.collection: Select Epigrams from the Greek Anthology (1890)
poems.text: If to die nobly is the chief part of excellence, to us out of all men Fortune gave this lot; for hastening to set a crown of freedom on Greece we lie possessed of praise that grows not old.

poems.title: On the Lacedaemonian Dead at Plataea (Mackail)
poems.author: Simonides of Ceos
poems.collection: Select Epigrams from the Greek Anthology (1890)
poems.text: These men having set a crown of imperishable glory on their own land were folded in the dark cloud of death; yet being dead they have not died, since from on high their excellence raises them gloriously out of the house of Hades.

poems.title: On the Same (Mackail)
poems.author: Simonides of Ceos
poems.collection: Select Epigrams from the Greek Anthology (1890)
poems.text: O passer by, tell the Lacedaemonians that we lie here obeying their orders.

poems.title: On the Athenian Dead at the Battle of Chalcis (Mackail)
poems.author: Simonides of Ceos
poems.collection: Select Epigrams from the Greek Anthology (1890)
poems.text: We fell under the fold of Dirphys, and a memorial is reared over us by our country near the Euripus, not unjustly; for we lost lovely youth facing the rough cloud of war.

poems.title: On the Same (Mackail)
poems.author: Simonides of Ceos
poems.collection: Select Epigrams from the Greek Anthology (1890)
poems.text: Cloudcapt Geraneia, cruel steep, would thou hadst looked on far Ister and long Scythian Tanaïs, and not lain nigh the surge of the Scironian sea by the ravines of the snowy Meluriad rock: but now he is a chill corpse in ocean, and the empty tomb here cries aloud of his heavy voyage.

poems.title: On a Thessalian Hound (Mackail)
poems.author: Simonides of Ceos
poems.collection: Select Epigrams from the Greek Anthology (1890)
poems.text: Surely even as thou liest dead in this tomb I deem the wild beasts yet fear thy white bones, huntress Lycas; and thy valour great Pelion knows, and splendid Ossa and the lonely peaks of Cithaeron.

poems.title: On Theognis of Sinope (Mackail)
poems.author: Simonides of Ceos
poems.collection: Select Epigrams from the Greek Anthology (1890)
poems.text: I am the monument of Theognis of Sinope, over whom Glaucus set me in guerdon of their long fellowship.

poems.title: On a Cretan Merchant (Mackail)
poems.author: Simonides of Ceos
poems.collection: Select Epigrams from the Greek Anthology (1890)
poems.text: I Brotachus of Gortyna, a Cretan, lie here, not having come hither for this, but for traffic.

poems.title: Snow in Summer (Mackail)
poems.author: Simonides of Ceos
poems.collection: Select Epigrams from the Greek Anthology (1890)
poems.text: With this once the sharp North Wind rushing from Thrace covered the flanks of Olympus, and nipped the spirits of thinly-clad men; then it was buried alive, clad in Pierian earth. Let a share of it be mingled for me; for it is not seemly to bear a tepid draught to a friend.

poems.title: Death at Sea (Mackail)
poems.author: Simonides of Ceos
poems.collection: Select Epigrams from the Greek Anthology (1890)
poems.text: Strange dust covers thy body, and the lot of death took thee, O Cleisthenes, wandering in the Euxine sea; and thou didst fail of sweet and dear home-coming, nor ever didst reach sea-girt Chios.

poems.title: Unforgotten (Mackail)
poems.author: Simonides of Ceos
poems.collection: Select Epigrams from the Greek Anthology (1890)
poems.text: Protomachus said, as his father held him in his hands when he was breathing away his lovely youth, "O son of Timenor, thou wilt never forget thy dear son, nor cease to long for his valour and his wisdom."

poems.title: On the Spartans
poems.author: Simonides of Ceos
poems.text:
These who with fame eternal their own dear land endowed
Took on them as a mantle the shade of death's dark cloud;
Yet dying thus they died not, on whom is glory shed
By virtue which exalts them above all other dead.

poems.title: On the Athenians
poems.author: Simonides of Ceos
poems.text:
If to die nobly be the meed that lures the noblest mind,
Then unto us of all men in this was fortune kind.
For Greece we marched, that freedom's arm should ever round her fold;
We died, but gained for guerdon renown that grows not old.
